title: Gingival Inflammation & Clinical Features of Gingivitis — Test

mcqs.q: The part of the attached gingiva boundary furthest from the teeth is the:
mcqs.explain: Attached gingiva extends from the free gingival groove to the mucogingival junction, where it meets the alveolar mucosa.

mcqs.q: Which feature is characteristic of HEALTHY gingiva?
opts: Smooth shiny surface with loss of stippling
mcqs.explain: Healthy gingiva is pink, scalloped, knife-edged, with firm papillae and physiologic stippling.

mcqs.q: The predominant inflammatory cell in the INITIAL lesion of gingival inflammation is the:
mcqs.explain: The initial lesion (2–4 days) is mainly vascular with neutrophils predominating; it is usually subclinical.

mcqs.q: The initial lesion of gingivitis appears at approximately:
mcqs.explain: Initial lesion 2–4 days; early lesion 4–7 days; established lesion 14–21 days.

mcqs.q: In the EARLY lesion (4–7 days), the predominant inflammatory cell becomes the:
mcqs.explain: Lymphocytes predominate in the early lesion; erythema and bleeding on probing may appear, and collagen destruction increases.

mcqs.q: The ESTABLISHED lesion (14–21 days) is characterised histologically by a predominance of:
mcqs.explain: Plasma cells predominate; vessels are engorged, a (pseudo)pocket may form, and localized anoxemia can give a bluish-red colour.

mcqs.q: The transition from gingivitis to periodontitis occurs in the:
mcqs.explain: The advanced lesion = periodontal breakdown: inflammation reaches deeper tissues with attachment loss and alveolar bone involvement.

mcqs.q: Which statement about gingivitis-to-periodontitis progression is correct?
opts: Not all gingivitis progresses to periodontal breakdown
mcqs.explain: Gingivitis may progress to periodontitis in susceptible individuals, but not all gingivitis progresses.

mcqs.q: The MOST commonly encountered type of gingivitis by course and duration is:
mcqs.explain: Chronic gingivitis (slow onset, long duration, painless) is the most common; acute is sudden, short and may be painful.

mcqs.q: Gingivitis described as involving the gingival margin, interdental papillae AND attached gingiva is classified by location as:
mcqs.explain: By location: marginal (margin), papillary (papillae), diffuse (margin + papillae + attached gingiva). Distribution is localized vs generalized.

mcqs.q: Early signs of gingivitis appear FIRST and most often at the:
mcqs.explain: The papillae are affected most often, and early gingivitis signs commonly appear there first.

mcqs.q: Which is considered the EARLIEST clinical sign of gingival inflammation?
opts: Bleeding on gentle probing / increased GCF
mcqs.explain: Increased GCF flow and bleeding on gentle probing are the earliest signs; BOP may precede a visible colour change.

mcqs.q: Absence of bleeding on probing (no BOP) is clinically valuable because it:
opts: Strongly indicates a lower future risk of attachment loss
mcqs.explain: No BOP is a strong indicator of periodontal stability (low future attachment-loss risk); persistent BOP indicates increased risk.

mcqs.q: Which factor SUPPRESSES gingival bleeding, potentially masking inflammation?
mcqs.explain: Smoking suppresses gingival bleeding; pregnancy, vitamin-C deficiency and aspirin tend to increase bleeding.

mcqs.q: Which is a LOCAL (plaque-retention) factor contributing to gingival bleeding?
mcqs.explain: Local plaque-retention factors include overhangs, malpositioned teeth, caries, appliances, partial dentures and frenum pull; hormones, diabetes and drugs are systemic.

mcqs.q: A patient on a calcium-channel blocker, an immunosuppressant, or aspirin illustrates gingival bleeding influenced by:
mcqs.explain: Calcium-channel blockers, immunosuppressants and aspirin are medications that can affect gingival bleeding/enlargement.

mcqs.q: A bluish-red gingival colour is most typical of:
mcqs.explain: Chronic inflammation and venous stasis give a bluish-red hue; acute redness is bright red, and severe acute necrosis gives greyish-white.

mcqs.q: A linear black discoloration of the gingival margin in a patient on systemic therapy is characteristic of:
mcqs.explain: Bismuth (heavy-metal) therapy causes a linear black gingival discoloration; amalgam tattoo is a localized grey area from embedded metal particles.

mcqs.q: In chronic gingivitis, a firm, leathery consistency indicates that the predominant process is:
mcqs.explain: Two processes may coexist: oedema → soft/swollen, and fibrosis → firm/leathery. A grayish slough and vesicles are features of acute forms.

mcqs.q: Loss of stippling with a smooth, shiny gingival surface reflects predominantly:
mcqs.explain: Smooth & shiny → exudative changes; firm & nodular → fibrotic; leathery → hyperkeratosis. Stippling gives the healthy ‘orange-peel’ look.

mcqs.q: Normally, the gingival margin is located relative to the CEJ approximately:
opts: At the level of the CEJ
mcqs.explain: The healthy margin sits ~1.5–2 mm above (coronal to) the CEJ. A coronal shift makes a pseudopocket; an apical shift beyond the CEJ is recession.

mcqs.q: Gingival recession is defined as apical displacement of the gingival margin, and clinically predisposes to all EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: Recession exposes the root → root caries, hypersensitivity and abrasion/erosion. A pseudopocket results from coronal (not apical) margin migration.

mcqs.q: Narrow triangular recession areas of the marginal gingiva that may widen and extend apically are called:
mcqs.explain: Stillman's clefts are narrow triangular recessions; McCall festoons are rolled, thick gingival bands near the canines — both linked to marginal inflammation.

mcqs.q: Rolled, thick, life-preserver-shaped gingival enlargements near the canines are termed:
mcqs.explain: McCall festoons are rolled thickenings of the gingival margin (often near canines) associated with recession approaching the mucogingival junction.

mcqs.q: A traumatic gingival lesion caused by aspirin, hydrogen peroxide or phenol is classified as:
mcqs.explain: Traumatic lesions are chemical (aspirin, H₂O₂, phenol, endodontic materials), physical (piercings, mechanical trauma) or thermal (hot foods/drinks).

mcqs.q: According to the hallmarks of gingivitis, the healthy contour ‘knife-edged and scalloped’ becomes:
mcqs.explain: In gingivitis, colour goes coral-pink→red, contour knife-edged→rolled with bulbous papillae, and consistency firm/stippled→soft/oedematous with loss of stippling.

mcqs.q: Continuous migration of neutrophils through the junctional epithelium into the sulcus is:
opts: A normal part of host defense
A sign of the advanced lesion only
mcqs.explain: In health, neutrophils continuously migrate through the junctional epithelium into the sulcus as part of normal host defense.

mcqs.q: A gingival (pseudo)pocket that may develop in the established lesion is due to:
opts: Coronal swelling of the gingival margin without attachment loss
Apical migration of the junctional epithelium
mcqs.explain: A pseudopocket forms from coronal enlargement/swelling of the margin; true (periodontal) pockets involve attachment loss seen in periodontitis.

mcqs.q: The attached gingiva extends from the:
opts: Free gingival groove to the mucogingival junction
Gingival margin to the free gingival groove
Cemento-enamel junction to the alveolar crest
Mucogingival junction to the vestibular fornix
mcqs.explain: The free (marginal) gingiva is the unattached terminal edge surrounding the tooth, and the interdental gingiva occupies the gingival embrasure between adjacent teeth.

mcqs.q: Colour changes in gingivitis usually BEGIN at the:
mcqs.explain: This matches the fact that the papillae are affected most often and show the early signs first.

mcqs.q: Which are the ENDOGENOUS causes of gingival colour change?
mcqs.explain: Tobacco (which increases melanin), heavy-metal pigmentation, amalgam tattoo and environmental or food pigments are the exogenous causes.

mcqs.q: Gingivitis that reappears after resolution is classified as:
mcqs.explain: Acute gingivitis has a sudden onset and short duration and may be painful; chronic gingivitis has a slow onset, long duration and is painless — and is the most common type.

saqs.q: Define gingiva and name its three anatomical parts.
saqs.a: The gingiva is the part of the oral mucosa covering the alveolar processes and surrounding the cervical portions of the teeth. Parts: FREE (marginal) — the unattached terminal edge; ATTACHED — bound to periosteum and bone, from the free gingival groove to the mucogingival junction; INTERDENTAL — occupying the gingival embrasure.

ans.text: The gingiva is the part of the oral mucosa that covers the alveolar processes of the jaws and surrounds the cervical portions of the teeth.

saqs.q: List the four stages of gingival inflammation with the predominant cell and approximate timing of each.
saqs.a: INITIAL (2–4 days) — vascular, PMNs predominate, subclinical, increased GCF. EARLY (4–7 days) — lymphocytes predominate, erythema and BOP, more collagen destruction. ESTABLISHED (14–21 days) — plasma cells predominate, chronic gingivitis, bleeding, pseudopocket, bluish-red. ADVANCED — breakdown into deeper tissues with attachment and bone loss.

saqs.q: What is bleeding on probing (BOP) and why is it clinically important?
saqs.a: BOP is bleeding from the sulcus on gentle probing — with increased GCF, the EARLIEST sign of inflammation, often preceding colour change. Useful for early detection, monitoring and prevention. ABSENCE strongly indicates lower future risk of attachment loss; PERSISTENT BOP indicates increased risk of attachment and tooth loss. Smoking suppresses bleeding and can mask inflammation.

ans.text: BOP — bleeding from the gingival sulcus on gentle probing. With increased GCF flow it is the earliest sign of gingival inflammation, and may precede a visible colour change.

ans.text: Useful for early detection, monitoring and prevention. Note that smoking suppresses gingival bleeding and can mask inflammation.

saqs.q: Classify the factors that contribute to gingival bleeding with examples.
saqs.a: LOCAL (plaque-retention) — anatomic/developmental variations, caries and malpositioned teeth, overhanging restorations, orthodontic appliances and retainers, partial dentures, recession or inadequate attached gingiva, frenum pull. SYSTEMIC — hormonal (puberty, pregnancy, menstrual cycle, oral contraceptives) and disorders (diabetes, platelet/coagulation disorders, vitamin-C deficiency). MEDICATIONS — calcium-channel blockers, immunosuppressants, aspirin.

saqs.q: Describe the clinical colour, consistency and surface-texture changes seen in gingival inflammation.
saqs.a: COLOUR — healthy pale/coral pink; inflammation gives redness (more vascularity, less keratinization); chronic venous stasis gives bluish-red; severe acute necrosis greyish-white; changes start at papillae and margin. CONSISTENCY — healthy firm and resilient; chronic may be soft/oedematous or firm/leathery (fibrosis); acute shows diffuse softening, greyish slough and vesicles. TEXTURE — healthy stippling ('orange peel'); smooth and shiny = exudative; firm nodular = fibrosis; leathery = hyperkeratosis.

saqs.q: Define gingival recession, state its clinical significance, and name the two contour changes associated with it.
saqs.a: GINGIVAL RECESSION — apical displacement of the gingival margin relative to the CEJ, exposing root surface; localized or generalized, increasing with age. SIGNIFICANCE — root caries, dentin hypersensitivity, root abrasion/erosion, difficult interproximal plaque control. CONTOUR CHANGES — Stillman's clefts (narrow triangular recessions) and McCall festoons (rolled thick bands, typically near the canines).

ans.text: GINGIVAL RECESSION — apical displacement of the gingival margin relative to the CEJ, exposing the root surface. May be localized or generalized, and increases with age.

rows: narrow triangular recession areas that may widen and extend apically
rolled, thick gingival bands, typically near the canines

ans.text: Both are linked to marginal gingival inflammation.
